synopsis: The next-generation CMS retains proximity warnings but adds automatic braking when the operator does not act; this is a different safety function, so matching the old warning system is not an adequate validation target [f12, f10417]. Automatic braking invalidates recorded replay at the first new brake command, making interactive closed-loop agreement important; a useful virtual environment therefore needs physically connected sensor, ground and object models, not merely a 3D scene [f108, f4813, f3904]. Major evidence gaps remain: no end-to-end heavy off-road vehicle-in-the-loop case, validated simulated braking distances on gravel, mud, ice or slopes, or off-road standard accepting simulation instead of physical braking tests was found [f342, f3970, f7539]. ISO 16001:2017 covers warnings rather than braking, and ISO 21815-4, listed for October 2026, excludes automatic brake application; South Africa was the only jurisdiction found to legally require automatic slowing and braking, while 2025 amendments to UN R152 permit virtual substitution for some car and van AEBS tests [f2070, f7543, f2077, f5162, f7546]. Prototype hardware and software are expected in mid-2027, but the organization has never developed this virtual-testing capability, and the research found no precedent for taking a new automatic-braking function from first representative hardware to accepted validation in about four months; every documented virtualization retained physical referents [f8250, f9401, f58, f10415]. Validation must address long stopping distances and legitimate work that resembles a collision, because false positives become machine-motion commands; available wheel-loader examples are limited to reverse operation, with Volvo CE's January 2023 system operating at 3–15 km/h for 2–3 seconds, and transferring road-vehicle evidence to quarry operations remains uncertain [f11381, f11384, f3024, f356, f11391, f11385].
